newsitem.title: GHANA: Rawlings and rival neck and neck in Ghana poll.
newsitem.headline: Rawlings and rival neck and neck in Ghana poll.

text.p: Ghana's populist president Jerry Rawlings and his main rival John Kufuor were neck and neck on Sunday as provisional results trickled in from presidential and parliamentary elections in the West African country.

Supporters of Rawlings, who twice seized power in the former British colony and has been called everything from a dictator to a messiah, took to the streets to celebrate after state radio announced landslide wins in his home Volta region in the east.

But Kufuor, a politician and businessman who was celebrating his 58th birthday on Sunday, enjoyed landslides of his own in constituencies in and around his stronghold of Kumasi, Ghana's second town and capital of the pre-colonial Ashanti empire.
"I am counting on at least 60 percent of the total votes to render a second round of no consequence," Rawlings, who is half-Scottish and still only 49, told Reuters on Sunday.
Provisional results from Saturday's elections showed that with about 12.5 percent of constituencies declared, Rawlings had 378,773 votes to Kufuor's 369,530.

In the contest for parliament's 200 seats, which was being tallied separately, Rawlings's National Democratic Congress had won 14 compared to 11 for the opposition alliance of Kufuor's New Patriotic Party and the People's Convention Party.

Ghanaians voted peacefully and in large numbers. National Election Commission chairman Kwadwo Afari-Gyan told Reuters on Sunday that the estimated turnout was 70 percent. More than nine million of Ghana's 17.5 million people were eligible to vote.

The Commonwealth Observer Group, among around 100 foreign observers monitoring the poll, paid tribute to the organisation and conduct of the election. "We believe that the conditions existed for a free expression of will by the electors," the 23-member mission said in a statement on Sunday.

Rawlings, bidding for a final four-year term as president, first seized power as an air force flight-lieutenant in 1979, executing three ex-heads of state. He restored civilian rule but seized power again in 1981.

A former socialist firebrand, he converted to Western-style free-market economics -- winning plaudits from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. He made the transition to elected president in disputed 1992 elections.

The main opposition, campaigning under the banner of the Great Alliance, learned the lesson of going into the 1992 multi-party elections in disarray and, against the odds, formed a common front for this year's elections.
Kufuor, who trained as a lawyer, has been campaigning for Ghanaians to have a greater stake in Ghana's economy, in which cocoa-growing and gold-mining are prominent.
A key question was whether Rawlings's crowd-pulling populism would bring him victory in the face of widespread unemployment and high inflation which have fuelled popular discontent.

Early results from the national election commission showed Employment and Social Welfare Minister David Sarpong Boateng losing his seat in parliament as did the government chief whip and a couple of regional ministers.
Political pundits said Rawlings appeared to be winning more of the rural vote, with Kufuor taking more of the urban vote.

They gave little chance to the third contender, surgeon Edward Mahama of the People's National Convention, but his presence could force a run-off, which must be held within 21 days in the event of no outright winner.
